queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the wildest-looking of the akou figs, roots poured over the walls and rock. It stands to the right of the main hall at Nojima Shrine, on the Nichinan coast road.
queue.story: Only one tree in this precinct is the national monument, and almost everybody gets it wrong. Nojima Shrine sits on the Nichinan coast road with akou figs all through it, roots poured over the walls and the rock, and the effect on arriving is unlike any other shrine grove in Japan, which is exactly why visitors assume the whole stand is protected. It is not. The designation, made in October 1941, covers the single tree standing to the right of the main hall: 6.9 metres round, 15 metres tall, put at 200 to 300 years by the Environment Agency. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the base, 12.9 metres round at chest height where the tree is still root, with the trunk proper narrower above it. It stands beside the walking path in Shiroyama Park.
queue.story: There is old forest 300 metres from Kagoshima's city hall because a lord gave up on a castle. A local clan built a fortress on this hill in the medieval period, which is where the name Shiroyama, castle hill, comes from. When the Shimazu took Kagoshima they built the flat, tower-less Tsurumaru castle at its northeastern foot instead, abandoned the hill fort within a generation, and closed the slope. Two and a half centuries of nobody going in produced what a 1974 academic survey counted as more than 510 species of higher plant on a hill 107 metres high, several of them recorded in Japan here for the first time.
